brief_item.title: Kairos让Prefill在Decode节点就地完成以删除跨节点KV传输
brief_item.core_conclusion: 解耦推理在突发负载下排队与KV传输占P95 TTFT近八成，把Prefill迁至空闲Decode节点既降时延又删传输。
brief_item.mechanism: 用分析式TBT模型估算迁后解码时延，仅当Decode路径不劣于原节点且仍在SLO内才偏转。
brief_item.result: 在2P2D A100上P95 TTFT最多降81%，SLO达成率升79%。
brief_item.boundary: 仅四卡小集群与单一MoE模型验证，未量化KV传输量也未处理前缀缓存。
brief_item.project_relevance: 这是GPU调度侧而非网络侧的优化，可作为规避KV传输的基准，不回答网络机制本身的不可替代价值。

facts.title: Towards Load-Aware Prefill Deflection for Disaggregated LLM Serving
facts.event_hint: Kairos: a load-aware prefill-deflection scheduler that runs deflected prefill in place on decode nodes to cut P95 TTFT up to 81% and eliminate inter-node KV-cache transfer in disaggregated LLM serving.
facts.problem: Disaggregated LLM serving runs prefill and decode on separate GPU pools, which creates a new asymmetry: under bursty, heavy-tailed workloads prefill nodes saturate and queue while decode nodes sit underutilized (decode is memory-bound with spare compute). On a 2P2D A100 cluster the authors show prefill execution is only 2-23% of P95 TTFT; the remaining 77-98% is prefill queue wait and inter-node GPU-to-GPU KV-cache transfer, both scheduling artifacts rather than compute limits. Prior disaggregated designs (Splitwise, DistServe, Mooncake, TetriInfer) assume a request stays on its prefill node until prefill completes and then ships its KV cache to a decode node, so they cannot exploit the spare compute on decode nodes.
facts.mechanism: Kairos is a proactive, time-aware prefill-deflection scheduler. For each queued request it estimates TTFT on the prefill node from current queue depth/order, and for every decode node sweeps candidate chunk-size sequences using an analytical TBT-safety model that predicts per-step decode latency from in-flight decode batch size, KV-cache occupancy, and added prefill chunk size (no live inference trials; one-time deployment-time profiling; no model changes). It deflects the request's prefill phase to a decode node when both (i) TBT safety holds (in-flight decode step latency stays within the TBT SLO tau, with margin beta) and (ii) projected decode-node TTFT is at most alpha times the prefill-node TTFT, where alpha >= 1 is a single operator-tunable knob (alpha=1 deflects only when the decode path is strictly faster). Algorithm 1 (PDF Page 9) formalizes this: build a TBT-safe chunk schedule per decode node via LargestSafe, pick the fastest feasible node, then deflect only if TTFT_dec(n*) <= alpha * TTFT_pf and TTFT_dec(n*) <= TTFT_slo (Eq. 7), else Keep. Deflected prefill runs as chunked-prefill steps interleaved with in-flight decode batches, so the prefill phase executes in place on the decode node and the inter-node KV-cache transfer is eliminated. Implemented on vLLM 0.18.1 (~2000 lines of Python); per-request scheduling overhead is below 1 ms at the prefill dispatcher.

evidence.claim: Prefill execution accounts for only 2-23% of P95 TTFT across the five workloads; the remaining 77-98% is prefill queue wait plus inter-node KV-cache transfer (e.g., Bursty: 840.8 ms prefill queue, 1,070.1 ms prefill exec, 2,175.6 ms KV transfer, 7,893.9 ms end-to-end P95).
evidence.baseline: Canonical 2P2D disaggregated serving (2 prefill + 2 decode nodes), no deflection
evidence.source_locator: Section 3.1 Claim 2 and Table 3, PDF Pages 4-5

evidence.claim: Kairos reduces P95 TTFT by up to 81% and raises SLO attainment by up to 79% over state-of-the-art disaggregated schedulers; the Section 6 evaluation names the baselines as PD Disaggregation (DistServe-style [21]) and TaiChi [18], run on the Bursty trace over RPS 6-12 where Kairos holds P95 TTFT/TBT SLO up to 9 RPS while PD disaggregation and TaiChi fall out earlier. Routing cost <1 ms per request.
evidence.value: up to 81% P95 TTFT reduction; up to 79% higher SLO attainment; <1 ms routing; SLO held to 9 RPS
evidence.condition: Bursty trace; RPS 6-12; SLO P95 TTFT<=4s and P95 TBT<=70ms; DeepSeek-V2-Lite; 2P2D A100 cluster; vLLM 0.18.1 (exact RPS/alpha of the 81%/79% maxima not stated in supplement)
evidence.source_locator: Abstract and Section 1, PDF Pages 1-2; Section 6.1.2 Baselines and 6.2/Figure 4, PDF Page 9

evidence.claim: Utilization is complementary: prefill SM utilization is 75-84% while decode SM utilization never exceeds 27%; the gap is widest in HPLD (84% prefill vs 7.5% decode), confirming decode-side compute slack available for chunked prefill.
evidence.condition: Five workloads; A100 80GB; measured via NVIDIA Nsight Systems
evidence.source_locator: Section 3 Claim 1 and Table 2, PDF Pages 3-4

evidence.claim: Injecting chunked prefill into decode batches keeps decode step-latency increase within 30 ms for chunk sizes up to 512 tokens across all workloads and batch sizes; for chunk sizes >= 1024 the first-chunk increase reaches about 30 ms (low-prefill regimes) up to about 50 ms (bursty/high-prefill regimes), so using large first chunks requires knowledge of cached-token volume.
evidence.value: delta T_step <= 30 ms for chunk size <= 512; up to ~50 ms for >= 1024
evidence.baseline: Decode step latency with no chunked-prefill injection
evidence.condition: Mixed prefill-decode batches on decode nodes across the five workloads

evidence.claim: Deflected requests execute prefill in place on the decode node, eliminating the inter-node KV-cache transfer; the system needs only one-time deployment-time profiling, no model changes, and imposes less than 1 ms per-request scheduling overhead (~2000 lines of Python on vLLM 0.18.1).
evidence.value: inter-node KV transfer eliminated for deflected requests; <1 ms routing; ~2000 LoC
evidence.baseline: Canonical disaggregated serving ships KV cache from prefill node to decode node
evidence.condition: Kairos on vLLM 0.18.1; 2P2D A100; deflected requests only
evidence.source_locator: Sections 1-2 Contributions and Design, PDF Pages 1-2; Algorithm 1, PDF Page 9

facts.evaluation_context: Section 6 evaluation runs on Azure Machine Learning Compute Clusters using Standard_ND96amsr_A100_v4 nodes, each with 8x NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs via NVLINK 3.0, AMD EPYC 7V12 64-core CPU, 900 GiB host memory; inter-node communication over InfiniBand and Azure Accelerated Networking. Topology is 2 prefill + 2 decode nodes (2P2D), with prior 1P3D / 3P1D comparisons on the Bursty workload. Model: DeepSeek-v2-Lite (MoE, 16B total / 2.4B active). Section 6 evaluates on the Bursty trace (most realistic, non-stratified) over RPS 6-12. SLO targets (both simultaneous): P95 TTFT <= 4 s, P95 TBT <= 70 ms. Section 6 baselines: PD Disaggregation (traditional DistServe-style [21], all prefill on prefill nodes) and TaiChi [18] (unified aggregation/disaggregation with differentiated GPU instances and flowing-decode scheduling). Q1 result: Kairos holds SLO up to 9 RPS while PD disaggregation and TaiChi fall out earlier. Per-request routing <1 ms; heartbeat interval = 100 ms; the decode-side single-deflection-per-heartbeat bottleneck requires RPS >= |decode nodes| / heartbeat (~20), far above the SLO-supported RPS, and is extensible by scaling decode nodes. Traces derived from a large-scale production LLM serving deployment (Company X); five workloads as in Table 1.
facts.limitations: The headline 'up to 81% TTFT / 79% SLO attainment' are best-case figures from the abstract/contributions; Section 6 confirms the baselines (PD Disaggregation/DistServe-style and TaiChi) and the Bursty/RPS 6-12 condition but does not state the exact alpha or RPS at which the 81%/79% maxima occur, and at lower request rates Kairos behaves similarly to standard PD disaggregation (little gain). Evaluated on a single small cluster (2P2D, four A100 nodes) and a single model architecture (DeepSeek-V2-Lite, MoE); the full throughput-vs-RPS curve (Figure 5) and any pool sizes beyond 2P2D are not in the supplement. Benefit depends on decode-side compute slack and workload regime, and using chunk size >= 1024 for the first chunk requires cached-token-volume awareness. New caveat from supplement: if a request has a prefix already cached on a prefill node, deflecting it to a decode node loses that cached prefix, and Kairos currently does NOT account for prefix-cache residency in its TTFT estimate. The evidence reports GPU SM/TC/HBM utilization but not aggregate KV-cache bytes transferred or network-bandwidth utilization as outcome metrics; KV-transfer reduction remains stated qualitatively (eliminated per deflected request), not quantified.
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to the TPN/KV-transfer topic: Kairos is a per-request, KV-cache-occupancy-aware scheduler that eliminates inter-node KV-cache transfer for deflected requests by running prefill in place on decode nodes, and it reports end-to-end P95 TTFT (up to 81% lower) and SLO attainment, which the topic values. Important boundary for project inference: Kairos is a GPU-pool/scheduling-side mechanism, not a network-side optimization; it avoids KV transfer rather than making the network faster, so it illustrates what scheduling alone can achieve and does not answer the topic's question about the irreplaceable value of network-side mechanisms. The visible evidence does not report network utilization, KV-transfer bytes, or TPOT as improved outcome metrics.
source_notes: Primary arXiv PDF (2607.02043v1) fetched; evidence covers abstract, intro/design (Pages 1-2), empirical study with Tables 1-3 and Figure 1 (Pages 3-5), and a partial throughput result (Page 10).
System is named Kairos in the body; the abstract describes it as a proactive prefill-deflecting scheduler.

Repair supplement (PDF Pages 9, 11, 12) added Algorithm 1 (deflection decision), Section 6 setup/baselines (PD Disaggregation = DistServe-style [21]; TaiChi [18]), the Bursty RPS 6-12 eval with Kairos holding SLO to 9 RPS, the decode-bottleneck threshold (RPS >= |decode nodes|/heartbeat ~20), and the prefix-cache-residency-loss caveat. It did not state the exact alpha/RPS of the 81%/79% maxima, did not show the Figure 5 throughput curve, and did not quantify KV-transfer bytes/network utilization.

evidence_gaps.question: Which specific disaggregated scheduler is the baseline for the up-to-81% TTFT and up-to-79% SLO-attainment results, and under which workload, RPS, and alpha are those maxima achieved (versus non-bursty or lower-load cases)?

Does the paper quantify the KV-cache transfer reduction (bytes or transfers eliminated) or network-bandwidth utilization as an outcome, rather than only stating per-deflected-request elimination and GPU SM/TC/HBM utilization?

What is the full throughput-vs-RPS curve (Figure 5 text is truncated at '7 RPS'), and at what load or cluster scale do Kairos gains over PD disaggregation vanish; are results shown beyond 2P2D / four A100s?

brief_item.title: GraphSpec把知识先验编译为运行期KV访问计划以压缩解码内存流量
brief_item.direction_name: 推理服务、运行时与编译优化
brief_item.core_conclusion: 知识增强LLM把图先验平铺成token迫使解码密集消费整段KV，KAP将其提升为运行期访问计划只暴露被选中的KV对象。
brief_item.mechanism: GraphSpec在vLLM分页KV上重排物理放置并保留逻辑位置，以同模型自推测解码验证全上下文。
brief_item.result: Qwen3-VL-32B上可见KV在128K仅5.5%，解码吞吐升1.08至1.19倍且质量不变。
brief_item.boundary: 仅Graph-RAG单实例验证，TTFT因编译略升，批次与并发未报告。
brief_item.project_relevance: 属解码期KV消费优化，与RAG缓存复用工作互补，长上下文多模态QA之外的可迁移性尚未证明。

facts.title: KAP: Bridging the Knowledge Selection-Runtime Consumption Gap in LLM Systems
facts.event_hint: QiYuanLab paper (arXiv:2607.24260v1, 2026-07-27) proposes Knowledge Access Planning (KAP), a serving-time IR that compiles structured knowledge priors into physical KV-access policies, instantiated as the GraphSpec compiler-executor on vLLM.
facts.problem: Knowledge-augmented LLM systems (RAG, GraphRAG, HippoRAG) produce rich structured priors (ranked evidence, graph topology, confidence), but prompt serialization collapses these into a flat token stream, forcing the serving backend to densely consume the full key-value (KV) state during decoding. The authors name this the Knowledge Selection-Runtime Consumption (KSRC) gap: richer contexts enlarge the KV footprint and decode-time memory traffic, raising latency and hurting throughput even when reasoning depends on a small fraction of the context.
facts.mechanism: KAP elevates structured knowledge priors from prompt-construction hints into first-class physical execution artifacts via a universal intermediate representation-the runtime access plan-that compiles knowledge signals to govern physical KV access without altering logical prompt semantics, model weights, or training. It is instantiated as GraphSpec: a compiler-executor pairing a Graph-RAG knowledge-selection frontend with a vLLM serving backend. Algorithm 1 (PDF Page 7) formalizes compilation: GroundEvidence -> AlignTokenSpans -> SelectEvidenceUnderBudget -> ResolveSelectedKVObjects -> PreserveLogicalPositions -> AssignCompactSlots -> BuildBlockTable/SlotMapping -> BuildSelectedKVView -> EmitRuntimeAccessPlan. The materialization reorganizes only physical KV placement over vLLM's paged-KV cache; original logical positions are preserved through the visibility mask, prompt-length metadata, block tables, and slot mappings consumed by the attention backend, so proposal and verifier logits stay aligned. The executor runs sparse self-speculative decoding with full-context verification using the SAME base model for proposal and verification (k=6 speculative tokens, q_prop=1 decode-like forward pass per proposal step); only the prompt-side KV objects exposed to attention are restricted by the selected-KV view. A phase-boundary cost model characterizes the positive-speedup regime via the margin h-s between proposal acceptance rate (h) and retained-KV ratio (s).

evidence.claim: GraphSpec reduces proposal-visible KV access from 40.1% of source KV at 4K down to 5.5% at 128K, with decode throughput (TPS) speedup rising from 1.08x to 1.19x over full-context vLLM as context grows.
evidence.condition: GraphSpec TPS 48.80 at 128K; long-context QA workload (SPIQA), 4K-128K; Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, 4xA800-80GB TP=4 bf16, vLLM v0.16.0, k=6 spec tokens; Graph-RAG priors frozen pre-benchmark; frontend retrieval excluded from TTFT

evidence.claim: Answer quality is preserved: pass-rate difference vs full-context is at most 0.3 percentage points at five of six lengths, and 1.9 points higher at 64K (87.9% vs 86.0%); average similarity stays closely matched (e.g., 0.748 vs 0.741 at 64K).
evidence.value: GraphSpec pass 87.9% vs 86.0% full-context at 64K; <=0.3pp gap elsewhere
evidence.baseline: Full-context decoding (same LLM-as-judge similarity metric, 0.5 threshold)
evidence.condition: 4K-128K context sweep on SPIQA; Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct; pass rate = fraction with weighted LLM similarity >= 0.5

evidence.claim: The runtime access plan, not evidence selection alone, drives the gain: materializing the same selected evidence as a 0.95K-token prompt (Physical concat) drops pass rate to 73.9% vs 87.9% for GraphSpec at 64K, while Random concat and Local window fall to 49.7% and 47.1%.
evidence.value: Physical concat 73.9% vs GraphSpec 87.9% pass at 64K
evidence.baseline: GraphSpec (full logical prompt preserved) vs Physical/Random/Local concat on vLLM
evidence.condition: 64K contexts on SPIQA; Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct; GraphSpec accessed KV/source 10.8%, TPS 51.70 vs full-context 45.68

evidence.claim: Empirical speedup tracks the phase-boundary prediction: retained ratio s falls from 0.401 to 0.055 across 4K-128K while acceptance h stays high (~0.95+), so the margin h-s rises from 0.557 to 0.897 alongside measured speedup rising 1.08x to 1.19x.
evidence.baseline: Phase-boundary cost model (directional implication, not refit to measurements)
evidence.condition: 4K-128K contexts on SPIQA; Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct; h = Top-3 tolerant proposal acceptance rate

evidence.claim: The LLM-as-judge pass criterion was independently audited: on 100 SPIQA samples, thresholded judge decisions agreed with majority-vote human labels on 95%; evidence recalls were answer 68.8%, rationale 66.8%, caption 76.8%.
evidence.baseline: Three independent human annotators, blinded to LLM scores, majority vote
evidence.condition: 0.5 threshold fixed before audit; token-level/ROUGE-1 coverage of gold evidence; Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct

facts.evaluation_context: Section 5.1 setup (PDF Page 11): target model is Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct (32B multimodal backbone); GraphSpec is implemented by extending VLLM v0.16.0. Hardware: four NVIDIA A800 80GB GPUs, tensor parallelism 4, bfloat16 execution; serving engine configured for the 4K-128K context sweep. GraphSpec uses the same base model for proposal and verification with k=6 speculative tokens (q_prop=1 per proposal step), i.e. sparse self-speculative decoding with full-context verification. Dataset: SPIQA, a multimodal QA benchmark grounded in figures, tables, and text from scientific papers, used for the FULL 4K-128K sweep (not only the 100-sample audit). Context-length control is a nested sweep: per query the answer and core supporting evidence are fixed and query-specific hard negatives are appended to build 4K/8K/16K/32K/64K/128K prompts; the distractor list is fixed across lengths. The full-context baseline, GraphSpec, and prompt-materialization baselines (Physical/Random/Local concat) share identical model weights, tokenizer, decoding config, software stack, and hardware. Graph-RAG priors frozen before benchmarking so frontend retrieval is excluded from TTFT; TTFT measured from frozen-request submission to first token and for GraphSpec includes runtime-access-plan compilation and selected-KV materialization; throughput covers the full executor path (not isolated model-forward). Quality via LLM-as-judge similarity in [0,1] with pass threshold 0.5. Audit dataset SPIQA. The supplement does NOT state batch size or request concurrency for the TPS/TTFT tables.
facts.limitations: Validates KAP through a single concrete instantiation (Graph-RAG frontend + vLLM v0.16.0 backend on Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, 4xA800-80GB TP=4 bf16); does not exhaust the broader design space. Results are strongest for long-context multimodal QA where graph-derived priors can be grounded in evidence spans and realized as backend runtime objects; effectiveness depends on prior quality, the compiler's translation, and backend execution without excessive metadata/scheduling/synchronization overhead. Gains are decode-throughput-only: GraphSpec TTFT is slightly higher than full-context at most lengths (e.g., 0.87s vs 0.65s at 8K, 1.56s vs 1.51s at 4K) due to plan-compilation overhead, only turning slightly favorable at 128K (37.90s vs 38.31s). The batch size and request concurrency used for the Tables 2-5 TPS/TTFT measurements remain unreported, so absolute throughput numbers cannot be re-scaled to other serving configurations.
facts.project_relevance: Falls in the serving/runtime/compiler direction: a serving-time IR and compiler-executor for plan-driven KV access, complementary to RAG serving cache-reuse work (RAGCache, CacheBlend, TurboRAG, RAGO) which targets prefill/scheduling/cache reuse rather than decode-time KV consumption. For our briefing it is a horizontal observation with measured but modest decode-throughput gains (1.08-1.19x) and a quality-preserving KV-reduction trajectory; deployability beyond Graph-RAG-style long-context QA is unproven.
source_notes: Primary source is arXiv:2607.24260v1 (FETCHED, raw_fulltext_cache_hit=true); evidence pack spans abstract/intro (p1), metrics+audit (p12), RQ1/RQ2 tables (p13), RQ3/RQ4 ablation+phase-boundary (p14), related work (p15), limitations+conclusion (p16).
GraphSpec speedups are decode-throughput (TPS); TTFT is generally not improved (plan-compilation overhead), an important boundary visible in Table 2.
Phase-boundary model is validated only directionally (not refit), per the authors' RQ4 design.

Repair supplement (PDF Pages 6, 7, 11) identified the previously-unknown setup: backbone Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct; SPIQA used for the full 4K-128K nested sweep; hardware 4xA800-80GB TP=4 bf16; vLLM v0.16.0; k=6 speculative tokens (q_prop=1); plus Algorithm 1 and the selected-KV-view materialization detail. Batch size / request concurrency remain unreported.

evidence_gaps.question: What GPU hardware, batch size, and request concurrency were used for the vLLM/GraphSpec throughput (TPS) and TTFT measurements, since these materially determine the absolute and relative numbers?

brief_item.title: AAFLOW+将KV缓存建模为分布式对象并按带宽决定传输或重算
brief_item.direction_name: KVCache感知的网络与带宽调度
brief_item.core_conclusion: 多Agent系统反复重算共享上下文且现有KV优化局限于单节点，AAFLOW+把KV提升为可跨Agent复用的分布式对象并提供派生与传输算子。
brief_item.mechanism: 构建通信感知工作流图，用UCX与NCCL零拷贝恢复已物化状态，带宽时延模型逐链路判定传输或重算。
brief_item.boundary: 结果为建模成本而非墙钟实测，10Gbps下8个场景中5个重算更优。
brief_item.project_relevance: 证实网络侧KV传输在中等以上带宽确有价值，低带宽交叉点是部署评估必须标注的边界。

facts.title: [AAFLOW+] Stateful Operator Abstraction with Zero-Copy Distributed KV Cache Orchestration for Multi-Agent Workflows
facts.event_hint: PVLDB/arXiv paper introducing AAFLOW+, a stateful agentic-workflow algebra that treats KV cache as a distributed object with materialize/transfer/fork/composition/eviction operators for multi-agent LLM serving.
facts.problem: Multi-agent LLM systems are text-centric: each agent repeatedly recomputes shared context via expensive prefill. Existing KV-cache optimization (vLLM PagedAttention, SGLang RadixAttention, DistServe, LMCache, FlexGen) is confined to single-node or single-request scopes and does not expose KV cache as a shareable distributed object across agents, so workflow-level branch duplication persists.
facts.mechanism: AAFLOW+ extends operator abstraction from dataflow to 'stateflow', making KV cache a first-class distributed systems object. It builds processes into communication-aware graphs that concurrently optimize data, prompts, and reusable model state, and provides explicit operators for KV materialization, transfer, fork, restricted composition, and eviction. The runtime enables zero-copy, transfer-aware execution so agents resume from already-materialized distributed state instead of replaying the prefix; communication uses UCX and NCCL. A bandwidth/latency-aware cost model decides transfer-vs-recompute per link.

evidence.claim: TTFT reduction (concrete): on the HF backend Mistral, AAFLOW+ reaches 0.041s mean TTFT vs AAFLOW-text 2.057s, dense prefill 2.017s, KVCOMM 0.704s, and DistServe-style 0.123s (3.0x slower). At vLLM max context Mistral AAFLOW+ is 0.171s vs dense prefill 38.880s and AAFLOW-text 39.655s.
evidence.value: 0.041s mean TTFT (HF Mistral); 0.171s at vLLM max context
evidence.baseline: DistServe-style 0.123s (3.0x slower); dense prefill 38.880s and AAFLOW-text 39.655s at vLLM max context
evidence.condition: HF/vLLM backends, Mistral-7B, 64 output tokens; Exp.1 bandwidth 200 Gbps, latency 50us

evidence.claim: Multi-agent scaling: at 16 agents AAFLOW+ gives 7.63x lower aggregate compute cost than the nearest competitor on Llama3 (220.05s vs SGLang-prefix 1679.81s) and 7.60x on Mistral (224.39s vs SGLang-prefix 1704.86s).
evidence.condition: HF backend, 16 agents, Mistral-7B / Llama-3-8B, 64 output tokens; aggregate modeled cost not wall-clock
evidence.source_locator: Section F.2 / Table 9, PDF Page 18; Table 3, PDF Page 10

evidence.claim: Transfer-vs-recompute crossover: KV transfer outperforms recomputation on moderate-to-high bandwidth; on slow 10 Gbps links recomputation is preferable for 5 of 8 contexts. The scheduler transfers state only when KV_bytes/bandwidth + latency < T_prefill.
evidence.value: recompute preferable in 5/8 contexts at 10 Gbps
evidence.condition: Exp.3 bandwidth sweep 10-400 Gbps, RDMA-like 10us / Ethernet-like 100us latency, HF backend Mistral

evidence.claim: Headline claims now located in supporting tables: 50.2x TTFT = Mistral AAFLOW-text 2.057s vs AAFLOW+ 0.041s (Exp.1, fixed 16 agents); KV-memory 1.72-6.10x spans vLLM-local 1.72x (14.351 GiB) to DistServe-style 6.10x (50.995 GiB) vs AAFLOW+ 8.355 GiB (Exp.4, branch factors 1-16); throughput 7.63-8.04x vs nearest competitors (Exp.5, 302.61 tok/s vs 37.62-39.62 tok/s), abstract states >7.74x.
evidence.baseline: AAFLOW-text 2.057s (50.2x); vLLM-local 14.351 GiB (1.72x) to DistServe 50.995 GiB (6.10x); SGLang/vLLM/DistServe 37.62-39.62 tok/s
evidence.condition: HF backend, Mistral-7B; Exp.1 fixed 16 agents / Exp.4 branch factors 1-16 / Exp.5 fixed context with variation agents
evidence.source_locator: Table 2, PDF Page 9; Table 4 + text, PDF Page 11 / Table 11, PDF Page 20; Table 5, PDF Page 11 / Table 12, PDF Page 20

facts.evaluation_context: Distributed GPU cluster of 4-16 nodes, each NVIDIA A100 (80GB and 40GB), 32-64 CPU cores, RDMA InfiniBand; communication via UCX/NCCL. Backends: HF (AutoModelForCausalLM, deterministic decoding), vLLM, SGLang. Models: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (up to 32,640 ctx) and Llama-3-8B-Instruct (up to 8,128 ctx), 64 generated tokens/branch. Workload is a shared-prefix parallel broadcast / Tree-of-Thought DAG (root -> KV materialize -> fork -> {agents} -> merge), not independent stateless chat; agent count swept k in {1,2,4,8,16}, context 1K-32K. Exp.1 network: 200 Gbps, 50us latency, 0.1ms resume overhead. Exp.3 sweeps 10-400 Gbps with 10us/100us latency. The total_latency_sec field is a modeled aggregate workload cost (text baselines charged 16x8x32=4096 full prefill/decode executions), explicitly NOT the Slurm wall-clock runtime. Throughput (Exp.5) and KV memory (Exp.4) are reported as modeled/simulated per-backend metrics over the same cost model.
facts.limitations: Results are from a trace-driven/analytical cost model parameterized by microbenchmarks, chosen to isolate systems-level KV-transfer limits from Python agentic-framework variance, not end-to-end observed wall-clock. The supplement confirms Exp.5 throughput and framework overhead remain a modeled/simulation profile (Omega is a modeled overhead), with no observed wall-clock validation. With Y=64 output tokens prefill dominates; if Y were thousands of tokens decode would dominate and the relative TTFT advantage shrinks. At 10 Gbps the serialized KV payload is large enough that recomputation wins for 5/8 contexts, so benefit requires moderate-to-high bandwidth. AAFLOW+ is not expected to help independent short stateless prompts (no shared state to fork/transfer).
facts.project_relevance: Directly on-topic for the TPN / state-aware-network card: it makes KV cache a distributed, network-transferable object with explicit transfer/fork operators and a bandwidth-aware transfer-vs-recompute scheduler, and reports the TTFT, throughput, KV-memory and transfer-crossover metrics the card lists as valuable evidence. It answers the card's core question by showing network-side KV transfer adds value beyond local GPU-memory scheduling, but only above a bandwidth crossover (it loses at 10 Gbps), which is exactly the applicability boundary the briefing must flag.

facts.title: Code Isn't Memory: A Structural Codebase Index Inside a Coding Agent
facts.event_hint: arXiv paper (SuperAGI Research) giving the first leak-audited, model-controlled causal ablation of a structural codebase index (semantic+lexical+call-graph) inside the open-source SuperCoder coding-agent harness, versus the same harness without it and an agentic-grep (OpenCode) comparator.
facts.problem: Coding agents interleave LLMs with repository retrieval, but retrieval implementations vary widely across harnesses and there is no clean causal answer to whether adding a structural codebase index changes cost or resolve. Prior work either compares whole harnesses (confounding retrieval with prompt, tool surface, and control loop) or evaluates retrieval components in isolation on acc@k without the downstream agentic loop that turns ranking into a fix.
facts.mechanism: Three arms run on the same instance set with the model held fixed (Claude Opus 4.7): SC-ON (SuperCoder harness with context-engine tools codebase_search and codebase_graph available), SC-OFF (same harness, same prompts, with exactly those two engine tools removed), and OpenCode (an independent harness whose retrieval is ripgrep + file reads, no structural index). The within-harness SC-ON vs SC-OFF toggle isolates the index causally. Localization is scored under 'View B' (agent-targeted), which strips paths whose only provenance is an engine result list so that SC-ON acc@k counts the same agent-targeted surface as a grep arm; the rule is a strict no-op for SC-OFF/OpenCode (Algorithm 1, §4.7).

evidence.claim: Within-harness ablation: View B acc@5 localization moves from 44.3% (SC-OFF) to 84.5% (SC-ON), paired Wilcoxon p < 0.0001.
evidence.condition: SuperCoder harness, Claude Opus 4.7, 3 seeds, View B localization, SWE-PolyBench Verified + SWE-bench Pro; pairwise n=80 (SC-ON vs SC-OFF)
evidence.source_locator: §7 Discussion, PDF Page 9; Table V, §6.2, PDF Page 7

evidence.claim: Within-harness ablation: resolve moves from 41.9% (SC-OFF) to 50.4% (SC-ON), paired p = 0.003; per-cell mean cost is statistically null (p = 0.73) while turns and tokens both fall significantly.
evidence.condition: same harness/model/seeds; resolve = F2P pass and P2P pass per upstream benchmark scorers
evidence.source_locator: §7 Discussion, PDF Page 9; Table V, §6.2, PDF Page 7

evidence.claim: Cross-harness check vs agentic-grep: SC-ON vs OpenCode on resolve (p = 0.087, delta +6.0 pp) and View B acc@5 (p = 0.080, delta +8.1 pp) is directional in SC-ON's favor but NOT conventionally significant (marginal). The within-harness ablation is the cleaner read.
evidence.condition: 3 seeds, pairwise n=78 (SC-ON vs OpenCode); across-seed SD 0.7-3.3 pp on resolve and acc@5, ablation effects exceed noise by 3-10x
evidence.source_locator: §7 Discussion / 'What we do not claim', PDF Page 9; §6.1, PDF Page 7

evidence.claim: Cost/effort: SC-ON $/solved is $2.30 vs SC-OFF $2.84 and OpenCode $2.92 (about 21% lower than OpenCode); per-cell mean cost is statistically null ($1.15 vs $1.19, p=0.73 within-harness; $1.15 vs $1.32, p=0.35 cross-harness). Turns drop from 36.2 to 28.3 (p<0.0001) and tokens from 11.1k to 10.1k (p=0.027) within-harness; cross-harness turns 36.0 to 28.3 (p<0.0001), tokens 14.0k to 10.1k (p<0.0001).
evidence.baseline: SC-OFF ($2.84/solved, 36.2 turns, 11.1k tokens) and OpenCode ($2.92/solved, 36.0 turns, 14.0k tokens)
evidence.condition: unified provider gateway captured token-level cost on every LLM call, same accounting across arms; per-cell means on legit cells, 3 seeds
evidence.source_locator: Table IV + Table V, §6.1-6.2, PDF Page 7; Abstract + §7 Discussion, PDF Pages 1 & 9

evidence.claim: Per-arm headline magnitudes (Table IV, mean of seed means): SC-ON resolve 50.4%, acc@5 84.5%, recall@5 0.611, $/solved $2.30, $/cell $1.15, turns 28.3, tokens 10.1k, wall-clock 4.5 min; SC-OFF resolve 41.9%, acc@5 44.3%, recall@5 0.330, $/solved $2.84, $/cell $1.19, turns 36.2, tokens 11.1k, wall-clock 5.5 min; OpenCode resolve 45.3%, acc@5 75.3%, recall@5 0.601, $/solved $2.92, $/cell $1.32, turns 36.0, tokens 14.0k, wall-clock 5.4 min. Per-seed resolve SD: SC-ON 2.75, SC-OFF 1.86, OpenCode 0.71 (Table III). First-gold-file rank-1 rate: SC-ON 77.4% vs OpenCode 58.4% vs SC-OFF 33.3% (Figure 3).
evidence.value: see claim; SC-ON cheaper iso-$/solved curve
evidence.condition: SC-ON/SC-OFF/OpenCode, Claude Opus 4.7, 3 seeds, SWE-PolyBench Verified + SWE-bench Pro; per-cell means on legit cells; acc@5 is View B
evidence.source_locator: Table III, Table IV, §6, PDF Page 7; Figure 3, PDF Page 8

facts.evaluation_context: Model fixed throughout: Claude Opus 4.7 (claude-opus-4-7), 3 seeds, pass@1 per seed; stats reported as mean of seed means with across-seed SD. Benchmarks: SWE-PolyBench Verified (Go, Java, Python) + SWE-bench Pro (long-context Python). Run scope: 91 instances (34 Go, 20 Java, 37 Python); JS/TS not covered. Paired-n: triple-intersection n=75; pairwise n=80 (SC-ON vs SC-OFF), n=78 (SC-ON vs OpenCode). 30-minute wall-clock cap, no turn/dollar cap; cap fired on two cells (one SC-OFF, one OpenCode); SC-ON's longest legit cell ran 19 min. Per-task isolated container, uniform image across arms, leak-audited sandbox; released artifacts include per-cell exclusion ledger, leak-audit script, dual-view localization extractor, and full results DB. Supplement (§6, PDF Pages 7-8) provides Table III (per-seed resolve), Table IV (headline metrics: resolve/acc@5/recall@5/$/solved/$/cell/turns/tokens/wall-clock per arm), Table V (causal ablation paired deltas and p-values), Table VI (per-language Go/Java/Python resolve and acc@5), Figure 3 (first-gold rank CDF: SC-ON rank-1 77.4% vs SC-OFF 33.3%), and Figure 4 (acc@5 by gold-file count: 3+ file bucket SC-ON 91.3% vs SC-OFF 44.9%, gap 46.4 pp). Exploratory per-language localization: Go 95.4% ON vs 44.8% OFF, Python 82.9% vs 42.4%, Java 71.7% vs 46.7% (Table VI; no significance claims, per-language n 18-46).
facts.limitations: Single-model study (only Claude Opus 4.7) — intentional control trade, acknowledged as a limitation. Closed-source harnesses (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf) out of scope by design. JavaScript/TypeScript not covered. The cross-harness SC-ON vs OpenCode result on resolve (p=0.087) and acc@5 (p=0.080) is marginal, NOT conventionally significant — the within-harness ablation is the cleaner read. The substantive benefit is conditional: the deployment question is whether the workload includes multi-file changes where structural ranking pays off (exploratory Figure 4 shows the largest within-harness acc@5 gap in the 3+ file bucket, 46.4 pp), not whether the index is too expensive to run. Per-language slices (Table VI) are exploratory with n=18-46 and no significance claims. Does not address the phrasing-ecological-validity threat (Garg et al. >50% capability overestimation).
facts.project_relevance: Directly on the Agent-semantic-acceleration card: it causally tests whether a structural codebase index reduces repeated search/read effort and improves task success, and reports exactly the card's valuable evidence — tool-call count (turns), token consumption, resolve rate, and $/solved. The supplement confirms the magnitudes: turns drop 36.2->28.3 (p<0.0001), tokens 11.1k->10.1k (p=0.027) within-harness while per-cell cost stays null ($1.15 vs $1.19, p=0.73) and $/solved drops to $2.30 from $2.84. This is concrete evidence that the index cuts repeated Read/Grep-style exploration, answering the card's core question. The marginal cross-harness result and single-model scope are the boundary the briefing must flag before generalizing.
source_notes: Source: arXiv 2606.22417v1, SuperAGI Research (Ishaan Bhola, Adithyan Krishnan, Sravanth Kurmala, Mukunda NS), fetch_status=FETCHED, raw_fulltext_cache_hit=true.

Evidence Pack spans PDF Pages 1, 2, 4, 5, 9: abstract, intro, related work, experimental design (arms/model/benchmarks/sandbox/metrics/localization views), and the §7 Discussion with the headline ablation numbers and explicit 'what we do not claim' caveats.

Repair supplement (PDF Pages 7-8) resolved the prior evidence gap: Table IV provides full per-arm headline metrics (turns 28.3/36.2/36.0, tokens 10.1k/11.1k/14.0k, $/solved $2.30/$2.84/$2.92, $/cell $1.15/$1.19/$1.32, wall-clock 4.5/5.5/5.4 min), Table V provides causal ablation paired deltas and p-values, Table III provides per-seed resolve, Table VI provides per-language breakdown, and Figures 3-4 provide rank CDF and gold-file-count heterogeneity.
